```{r}

#| include: false
post_dir <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir=TRUE),mustWork=TRUE))
snapshot <- read.csv(file.path(post_dir,'results/render_manifest.csv'))
stopifnot(identical(unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(post_dir,snapshot$file))),snapshot$md5))
source(file.path(post_dir,'scripts/figures.R'),local=knitr::knit_global())
fmt <- function(x)sprintf('%.2f',x)

fragment <- function(name)cat(readLines(file.path(post_dir,'includes',name),warn=FALSE),sep='\n')
```

**A sample mean differs from zero. Is that enough evidence that the population mean differs from zero?** The estimate alone does not tell us how much it might change across samples. Three simulations make that uncertainty visible: resample one dataset, repeat the entire sampling process, then ask what a zero-mean population would produce.

I generate independent observations from a normal population with **mean 3** and **standard deviation 20**. The mean is small relative to the spread, so sampling variation can obscure it. We know the true mean because we generated the population; the sample-based analysis treats it as unknown. That distinction lets us check the inference against a known answer.

## Build an interval from one sample

Draw **200 observations**. Their sample mean is **`r fmt(case$mean)`**, rather than exactly 3. For the bootstrap, draw 200 values **with replacement** from this observed sample and calculate their mean. Repeat 9,999 times. Some observations appear more than once in a resample and others are omitted. Figure 1 plots the resulting distribution of means.

For a [**95% percentile bootstrap interval**](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html), use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of those means. The default interval is **`r fmt(default$low)` to `r fmt(default$high)`**. The interval includes zero as well as positive and negative values, so the sample does not pin down the sign of the population mean.

The controls update all three figures. Increasing the confidence level widens intervals. Changing sample size also changes the observations, so the estimated mean can move even as precision generally improves.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('controls.html')
fragment('bootstrap.html')
```

## Check what 95% confidence means

One interval cannot show how frequently the procedure succeeds. Draw **2,000 new samples** from the population with mean 3. For each new dataset, construct a separate percentile interval using 999 bootstrap resamples. This repeats both sampling and interval construction, rather than repeatedly bootstrapping the original dataset.

At the default settings, **`r default$covered` of 2,000 intervals contain 3: `r percent(default$coverage)`**. Figure 2 shows the first 100 in their original order, with misses highlighted. The true mean remains fixed while the intervals move. The 95% label concerns coverage across repeated samples, not a 95% probability assigned to the fixed mean after one interval is observed.

Coverage is approximate. With 50 observations, **`r sprintf('%.2f%%',100*all_data$cases[['50']]$levels[['95']]$coverage)`** of the intervals cover 3 in this experiment. More bootstrap repetitions can stabilize estimated quantiles, but do not increase the number of independent observations in a sample.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('coverage.html')
```

## Simulate the evidence against a zero mean

Now test $H_0:\mu=0$ against a difference in either direction. Use $t=\bar{x}/(s/\sqrt{n})$, where $s$ is the sample standard deviation. This expresses the sample mean's distance from zero in standard-error units. The default statistic is **`r fmt(case$t)`**.

Generate **50,000 new samples under the null**, changing the population mean to zero while retaining the normal model and standard deviation 20. Calculate t for each sample. Figure 3 shows this null distribution. At a 5% significance level, reject when $|t|$ exceeds approximately **`r fmt(default$critical)`**. The two rejection tails together contain about 5% of null statistics.

About **`r percent(case$tail_count/all_data$D)`** of the null statistics lie at least as far from zero as the observed statistic, giving a [Monte Carlo p-value](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.monte_carlo_test.html) of approximately **`r sprintf('%.3f',case$p)`**. We therefore do not reject a zero population mean at the 5% significance level. Switch the shading to compare the p-value tails with the rejection regions. Changing the significance level moves the rejection boundaries, but leaves this sample's p-value unchanged. That p-value describes outcomes under the null, not the probability that the null is true.

```{r}
#| results: asis
fragment('null.html')
```

## Takeaway

The observed mean, **`r fmt(case$mean)`**, differs from zero, but the interval spans zero and the test does not reject a zero population mean—even though the population mean is 3. Failing to reject therefore does not establish a zero mean. Meanwhile, **`r sprintf('%.2f%%',100*default$coverage)`** repeated coverage illustrates what the interval's 95% label describes. The three simulations answer different questions: uncertainty from one sample, interval performance across samples, and surprise under a specified null.
